cards.q: When does the cardiovascular system develop?
cards.a:
**From about 18 days to 12 weeks — it is the earliest functional system in the body.**

## Understanding it
- The CVS is the **first** organ system to function (~18 days), completing by ~12 weeks.

>> 18 days–12 weeks; the earliest functional system.
opts: 18 days to 12 weeks — the earliest functional system

cards.q: Why does the CVS form so early?
cards.a:
**Because the embryo has grown too big for simple diffusion to meet its oxygen/nutrient needs, so it needs circulation.**

## Understanding it
- Once the embryo outgrows **diffusion distances**, it must have a working circulation.

>> Diffusion can no longer supply the growing embryo.
opts: Diffusion can no longer meet the growing embryo's needs
To make the heart beat for fun

cards.q: List the five sources of the CVS.
cards.a:
**Splanchnic mesoderm; paraxial and lateral mesoderm; otic placodes; neural crest cells; and (endothelial) precursors.**

## Understanding it
- The CVS draws on several sources — chiefly **splanchnic mesoderm** (heart) and **neural crest** (outflow tract).

>> Splanchnic + paraxial/lateral mesoderm, otic placodes, neural crest.
opts: Splanchnic mesoderm, paraxial/lateral mesoderm, otic placodes, neural crest

cards.q: What does splanchnic mesoderm contribute to the heart?
cards.a:
**The primordium (foundation) of the heart — heart muscle and lining.**

## Understanding it
- Splanchnic mesoderm forms the **heart muscle and endocardial lining**.

>> Splanchnic mesoderm → heart muscle and lining.
opts: The heart primordium — muscle and lining

cards.q: What do the paraxial and lateral mesoderm contribute?
cards.a:
**Blood vessel walls and connective tissue.**

## Understanding it
- These mesoderms build **vessel walls and connective tissue** (not the heart muscle itself).

>> Vessel walls and connective tissue.
opts: Blood vessel walls and connective tissue

cards.q: What do neural crest cells contribute?
cards.a:
**Outflow tract septation and the great-vessel walls — defects here cause cono-truncal anomalies (TGA, TOF, truncus).**

## Understanding it
- Neural crest builds the **outflow tract septum and great-vessel walls**; their failure causes the classic cono-truncal defects.

>> Outflow tract septation and great-vessel walls.
opts: Outflow tract septation and great-vessel walls

cards.q: What are the two most important sources to remember and their products?
cards.a:
**Splanchnic mesoderm (heart muscle and lining) and neural crest cells (outflow tract septation and great vessels).**

## Understanding it
- Remember the pair: **splanchnic mesoderm = the heart**; **neural crest = the outflow tract**.

>> Splanchnic (heart) + neural crest (outflow tract).
opts: Splanchnic mesoderm (heart) and neural crest (outflow tract)

cards.q: What are myoblasts?
cards.a:
**Cardiac progenitor cells (future heart-muscle cells) that cluster in the cardiogenic field.**

## Understanding it
- Myoblasts are the **early heart-muscle precursors**.

>> Myoblasts = cardiac muscle progenitor cells.

cards.q: What are angioblastic cords?
cards.a:
**Cord-like structures formed by the myoblasts, which hollow out and fuse to form the heart tube/vessels.**

## Understanding it
- Angioblastic cords **hollow out and fuse** into the primitive heart tube and vessels.

>> Cords that hollow/fuse into the heart tube.
opts: Cords that hollow out and fuse into the heart tube

cards.q: Where is the cardiogenic field located?
cards.a:
**Anterior (in front) to the endodermal primitive pharynx, initially cephalad (head end) to the embryo.**

## Understanding it
- It begins **at the head end**, in front of the pharynx, before folding brings it to the chest.

>> In front of the pharynx, initially cephalad.
opts: Anterior to the primitive pharynx, initially cephalad

cards.q: Why does the heart end up in the chest despite starting cephalad?
cards.a:
**Because the embryo folds craniocaudally in weeks 3–4, carrying the heart down into the thorax.**

## Understanding it
- **Craniocaudal folding** relocates the head-end heart into the chest.

>> Craniocaudal folding carries the heart into the thorax.
opts: It grows a new heart in the chest
Craniocaudal folding carries it into the thorax
The heart migrates through the blood

cards.q: When does the primitive heart tube form and from what?
cards.a:
**By the 4th week, from the two angioblastic cords hollowing out and fusing.**

## Understanding it
- The single heart tube forms by **week 4** from fused angioblastic cords.

>> Week 4, from fused angioblastic cords.
opts: By week 4, from two fused angioblastic cords

cards.q: What anchors the caudal (lower) end of the heart tube?
cards.a:
**The septum transversum (a mesoderm block that helps form the diaphragm).**

## Understanding it
- The **caudal** end is fixed by the **septum transversum**.

>> Caudal anchor = septum transversum.

cards.q: What anchors the cephalad (upper) end of the heart tube?
cards.a:
**The six arterial (aortic) arches.**

## Understanding it
- The **cephalad** end is fixed by the **six arterial arches**.

>> Cephalad anchor = the 6 arterial arches.

cards.q: When does dilatation of the heart tube become visible?
cards.a:
**Days 21 to 24.**

## Understanding it
- The tube's regional dilatations appear around **days 21–24**.

>> Days 21–24.

cards.q: What will the venous (caudal) end of the heart tube become?
cards.a:
**The atria.**

## Understanding it
- The **venous (caudal)** end forms the **atria**.

>> Venous end → atria.

cards.q: What will the arterial (cephalad) end of the heart tube become?
cards.a:
**The ventricles and outflow tract.**

## Understanding it
- The **arterial (cephalad)** end forms the **ventricles and outflow tract**.

>> Arterial end → ventricles and outflow tract.

cards.q: Why does the heart tube loop?
cards.a:
**Because it is anchored at both ends in the limited pericardial cavity and grows faster than the space allows, so it bends/loops.**

## Understanding it
- Fixed ends + rapid growth in a small space force the tube to **loop**.

>> Fixed ends + fast growth in small space → looping.
opts: The blood pushes it into a loop
It is fixed at both ends and outgrows the pericardial space

cards.q: What abnormality results from looping in the wrong direction?
cards.a:
**Dextrocardia (heart on the wrong side).**

## Understanding it
- Looping to the **left instead of right** gives **dextrocardia**.

>> Wrong-direction looping → dextrocardia.

cards.q: Describe stage 1 of looping (atrial looping).
cards.a:
**A right-angle bend between the primitive atrium and the interventricular region.**

## Understanding it
- Stage 1 = a **right-angle bend** at the atrial/interventricular junction.

>> Stage 1 = a right-angle atrial bend.
opts: A right-angle bend between atrium and interventricular region

cards.q: Describe stage 2 of looping (ventricular looping).
cards.a:
**A dramatic 180-degree flexure between the interventricular region and the bulbus cordis.**

## Understanding it
- Stage 2 = a **180° flexure** that positions the ventricles.

>> Stage 2 = a 180° ventricular flexure.
opts: A straight tube with no flexure
A 180° flexure between interventricular region and bulbus cordis

cards.q: What does looping achieve overall?
cards.a:
**It repositions the atria behind and above the ventricles, with the ventricles side by side — the mature spatial arrangement.**

## Understanding it
- Looping puts **atria behind/above, ventricles below** — the adult layout.

>> Atria behind/above; ventricles side by side.
opts: The heart on the right side
Atria behind/above the ventricles; ventricles side by side

cards.q: What problem do convergence and wedging solve?
cards.a:
**After looping, the inlets and outlets are not yet aligned over their correct ventricles — convergence and wedging align them.**

## Understanding it
- These movements **align the inlets/outlets** over the proper ventricles.

>> They align inlets/outlets with the correct ventricles.
opts: Aligning the inlets and outlets over the correct ventricles

cards.q: What is convergence?
cards.a:
**The AV canal (inlet) and bulbus cordis (outlet) move closer toward each other/the midline.**

## Understanding it
- Convergence brings the **inlet and outlet closer** together.

>> Inlet (AV canal) and outlet (bulbus) move together.
opts: The AV canal (inlet) and bulbus cordis (outlet) move closer together

cards.q: Describe wedging.
cards.a:
**A two-part movement: the AV canal shifts to the right so each AV orifice sits over its own ventricle, and the aorta wedges between the two AV valves.**

## Understanding it
- Wedging positions each **AV valve over the right ventricle** and slots the **aorta between them** (over the LV).

>> AV canal shifts right; aorta wedges between the AV valves.
opts: AV canal shifts right and the aorta wedges between the AV valves

cards.q: After wedging, over which ventricles do the valves and great vessels sit?
cards.a:
**Tricuspid over the RV, mitral over the LV, and aorta over the LV (wedged between the AV valves).**

## Understanding it
- Correct alignment: **tricuspid→RV, mitral→LV, aorta→LV**.

>> Tricuspid→RV, mitral→LV, aorta→LV.
opts: Tricuspid over RV, mitral over LV, aorta over LV
Both great vessels over the LV

cards.q: What defect results from failed wedging?
cards.a:
**Double Outlet Right Ventricle (DORV) — both the aorta and pulmonary trunk arise over the RV.**

## Understanding it
- Failed wedging leaves **both great arteries over the RV** = DORV.

>> Failed wedging → DORV.

cards.q: What defect results from abnormal convergence?
cards.a:
**Double Inlet Left Ventricle (DILV) — both AV valves drain into the LV.**

## Understanding it
- Abnormal convergence sends **both AV valves into the LV** = DILV.

>> Abnormal convergence → DILV.

cards.q: Which three paired veins drain into the sinus venosus?
cards.a:
**The vitelline vein, the umbilical vein, and the common cardinal vein.**

## Understanding it
- Three venous inputs: **vitelline (yolk sac), umbilical (placenta), cardinal (body)**.

>> Vitelline, umbilical, common cardinal veins.
opts: Vitelline, umbilical, and common cardinal veins

cards.q: What is the function and adult fate of the vitelline vein?
cards.a:
**Returns deoxygenated blood from the yolk sac; becomes the hepatic veins, portal system and part of the IVC.**

## Understanding it
- Vitelline vein → **hepatic/portal system** (and part of the IVC).

>> Yolk-sac drainage; becomes hepatic/portal veins.
opts: Carries placental blood; becomes ductus venosus
Drains the yolk sac; becomes hepatic/portal veins (and part of IVC)
Drains the head; becomes the SVC

cards.q: What is the function of the umbilical vein and why is it unusual?
cards.a:
**It carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the embryo — unusual because veins usually carry deoxygenated blood.**

## Understanding it
- The umbilical **vein carries OXYGENATED** placental blood — the exception to the vein rule.

>> Umbilical vein carries oxygenated placental blood (a vein exception).
opts: Carries oxygenated placental blood (unusual for a vein)
Carries deoxygenated blood from the body
Carries deoxygenated blood from the yolk sac

cards.q: What is the adult fate of the umbilical vein?
cards.a:
**It forms the ductus venosus, which becomes the ligamentum venosum at birth.**

## Understanding it
- Umbilical vein → **ductus venosus** → **ligamentum venosum** after birth.

>> Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum.
opts: Forms the ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum

cards.q: What is the role of the ductus venosus?
cards.a:
**It allows oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass the liver and go straight to the IVC/heart.**

## Understanding it
- The ductus venosus is a **liver bypass** for oxygenated placental blood.

>> Bypasses the liver to the IVC.
opts: Lets placental blood bypass the liver to the IVC

cards.q: What does the common cardinal vein return, and what does it form?
cards.a:
**Deoxygenated blood from the body; it forms the SVC and IVC (systemic venous return).**

## Understanding it
- The cardinal system drains the **body** and forms the great systemic veins (**SVC/IVC**).

>> Drains the body; forms the SVC and IVC.
opts: Drains the yolk sac; forms the portal vein
Drains the body; forms the SVC and IVC
Drains the placenta; forms the ductus venosus

cards.q: What two tributaries form each common cardinal vein?
cards.a:
**The anterior cardinal vein (drains the head) and the posterior cardinal vein (drains the body/trunk).**

## Understanding it
- **Anterior cardinal = head; posterior cardinal = body**, joining as the common cardinal.

>> Anterior (head) + posterior (body) cardinal veins.

cards.q: What is the adult fate of the right anterior cardinal vein?
cards.a:
**It becomes the superior vena cava (SVC).**

## Understanding it
- The **right** anterior cardinal vein → **SVC** (right-sided dominance).

>> Right anterior cardinal → SVC.

cards.q: What is the fate of the left anterior cardinal vein?
cards.a:
**It largely regresses.**

## Understanding it
- The **left** anterior cardinal vein mostly **disappears** (failure to regress → persistent left SVC).

>> Left anterior cardinal largely regresses.

cards.q: From how many segments is the IVC assembled, and name them.
cards.a:
**Four: hepatic veins, right subcardinal vein, right supracardinal vein, and a hepatic segment (from the vitelline system).**

## Understanding it
- The IVC is a **composite of four segments**, which is why segmental failure causes anomalies.

>> Four segments (hepatic, subcardinal, supracardinal, etc.).

cards.q: Give examples of IVC anomalies from segmental failure.
cards.a:
**Absent infrarenal IVC, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, and double IVC.**

## Understanding it
- Because it is built from segments, the IVC can be **absent, interrupted (azygos continuation), or doubled**.

>> Absent, interrupted (azygos continuation), or double IVC.
opts: Absent infrarenal IVC, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, double IVC

cards.q: What is the recurring theme of systemic venous development?
cards.a:
**Right-sided dominance — the right cardinal system forms the SVC and IVC while the left largely regresses.**

## Understanding it
- The **right** venous channels persist; the **left** regress — 'right-sided dominance'.

>> Right-sided dominance of the venous system.

cards.q: Why can the atria not be completely sealed in fetal life?
cards.a:
**Because the fetus does not use its lungs; oxygenated placental blood must cross from right to left through the atrial septum.**

## Understanding it
- With the lungs bypassed, blood must **shunt right→left** across the atria (via the foramen ovale).

>> Fetal lungs are bypassed → right-to-left atrial shunt needed.
opts: To let deoxygenated blood into the aorta
The atria never form a septum
The fetus bypasses the lungs, so blood must shunt right→left across the atria

cards.q: How does septum primum grow, and what gap does it leave?
cards.a:
**It grows down from the roof of the atrium toward the endocardial cushions, leaving a gap below it called the foramen primum.**

## Understanding it
- Septum primum descends, and the gap beneath it is the **foramen primum**.

>> Grows down from the roof; leaves the foramen primum.
opts: Grows down from the roof, leaving the foramen primum below
Grows up from the floor, leaving the foramen ovale

cards.q: How does the foramen secundum form?
cards.a:
**As septum primum reaches the floor and closes the foramen primum, perforations appear high in septum primum, coalescing into the foramen secundum.**

## Understanding it
- As the foramen primum closes, **holes high in septum primum** merge into the foramen secundum (keeping the shunt open).

>> Perforations high in septum primum coalesce → foramen secundum.
opts: Perforations high in septum primum coalesce into the foramen secundum

cards.q: Describe septum secundum.
cards.a:
**An invagination of the atrial roof growing down to the right of septum primum, thick and muscular.**

## Understanding it
- Septum secundum is a **thick, muscular** partition to the **right** of septum primum.

>> Thick muscular septum, right of septum primum.
opts: A thin flap left of septum primum
A thick muscular partition growing down right of septum primum

cards.q: Why is septum secundum thicker and more muscular than septum primum?
cards.a:
**To withstand the higher pressure and blood flow in the right atrium during fetal life.**

## Understanding it
- The **right atrium is higher-pressure** in the fetus, so septum secundum is built stronger.

>> To withstand higher right-atrial pressure.
opts: To withstand higher right-atrial pressure and flow

cards.q: What is the foramen ovale?
cards.a:
**The gap left because septum secundum grows down but stops short of the endocardial cushions (offset from the foramen secundum).**

## Understanding it
- The foramen ovale is the **incomplete gap in septum secundum**, offset from septum primum's opening — forming a flap valve.

>> The incomplete gap in septum secundum (a flap valve with septum primum).
opts: A hole in the endocardial cushion
The gap where septum secundum stops short (a flap valve)

cards.q: In fetal life, why is the foramen ovale open?
cards.a:
**Right atrial pressure exceeds left (lungs not working), pushing septum primum aside so blood shunts right to left.**

## Understanding it
- Higher **right-atrial pressure** holds the flap open, allowing the essential right→left shunt.

>> High RA pressure holds the flap open (right→left shunt).
opts: High right-atrial pressure holds the flap open (right→left shunt)

cards.q: At birth, why does the foramen ovale close?
cards.a:
**The first breath expands the lungs, pulmonary pressure drops, left atrial pressure rises above the right, pressing septum primum against septum secundum.**

## Understanding it
- Breathing reverses the pressure gradient → **left > right**, sealing the flap.

>> First breath → LA pressure > RA → flap seals.
opts: The first breath raises LA pressure above RA, sealing the flap

cards.q: What does the foramen ovale become in the adult?
cards.a:
**The fossa ovalis (after the two septa fuse).**

## Understanding it
- The closed foramen ovale leaves the **fossa ovalis** on the atrial septum.

>> Fossa ovalis.

cards.q: What are the endocardial cushions, and what three things do they contribute to?
cards.a:
**Masses of tissue in the AV canal region; they help close the foramen primum, divide the AV canal into two orifices, and contribute to the AV valves and membranous septum.**

## Understanding it
- The endocardial cushions build the **AV septum, AV valves, and part of the membranous ventricular septum**.

>> Close foramen primum; split the AV canal; form AV valves/membranous septum.
opts: Close the foramen primum, split the AV canal, form AV valves/membranous septum

cards.q: What defect results from endocardial cushion failure, and which syndrome is it associated with?
cards.a:
**Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), commonly associated with Down syndrome.**

## Understanding it
- Failed cushions → **AVSD**, classically in **Down syndrome**.

>> AVSD (endocardial cushion defect), linked to Down syndrome.

cards.q: What causes ASD secundum, the most common ASD?
cards.a:
**Excessive resorption of septum primum, or a foramen ovale that is too large (septum secundum too small).**

## Understanding it
- Secundum ASD = **too much septum primum resorption or too-large foramen ovale**.

>> Excess septum primum resorption / too-large foramen ovale.
opts: Failure of septum primum to fuse with cushions
Excess resorption of septum primum or a too-large foramen ovale

cards.q: What causes ASD primum?
cards.a:
**Failure of septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions.**

## Understanding it
- Primum ASD = **septum primum doesn't fuse with the cushions** (near the AV valves; overlaps AVSD spectrum).

>> Septum primum fails to fuse with the cushions.
opts: Failure of septum primum to fuse with the endocardial cushions

cards.q: What causes a patent foramen ovale, and how common is it?
cards.a:
**The septa form but never permanently fuse; present in about 25% of adults.**

## Understanding it
- PFO = the flap **never fully seals**; common (**~25%**) and often benign.

>> Septa don't fuse; ~25% of adults.
opts: The septa never permanently fuse; ~25% of adults
Complete absence of the septa; rare

cards.q: What causes a common atrium?
cards.a:
**Complete failure of atrial septation (no septum forms).**

## Understanding it
- A single common atrium = **total failure of septation**.

>> Complete failure of atrial septation.
opts: Failure of septum primum to fuse with cushions

cards.q: What are the two horns of the sinus venosus and their broad fates?
cards.a:
**The right horn is absorbed into the right atrium; the left horn shrinks to form the coronary sinus (and oblique vein of the left atrium).**

## Understanding it
- **Right horn → right atrium (smooth part); left horn → coronary sinus** (right-sided dominance again).

>> Right horn → RA; left horn → coronary sinus.
opts: Right horn → right atrium; left horn → coronary sinus
Left horn → right atrium; right horn → coronary sinus

cards.q: What does the left sinus horn form?
cards.a:
**The coronary sinus and the oblique vein of the left atrium.**

## Understanding it
- The **left** sinus horn → **coronary sinus** (+ oblique vein of the LA).

>> Left sinus horn → coronary sinus.
opts: The coronary sinus (and oblique vein of the left atrium)

cards.q: What does the right sinus horn form?
cards.a:
**The smooth-walled sinus venarum of the right atrium and the valve of the IVC/SVC.**

## Understanding it
- The **right** sinus horn → **smooth part (sinus venarum) of the RA**.

>> Right sinus horn → smooth-walled RA (sinus venarum).
opts: The smooth-walled sinus venarum of the right atrium

cards.q: What are the two parts of the adult right atrium and their origins?
cards.a:
**The rough/trabeculated part (pectinate muscles) from the primitive atrium; and the smooth part (sinus venarum) from the absorbed right sinus horn.**

## Understanding it
- RA = **rough (primitive atrium) + smooth (right sinus horn)**, separated by the crista terminalis.

>> Rough (primitive atrium) + smooth (right sinus horn).
opts: Rough from the sinus horn; smooth from primitive atrium
Both parts from the sinus venosus
Rough part from the primitive atrium; smooth part from the right sinus horn

cards.q: What is the crista terminalis?
cards.a:
**The muscular ridge marking the internal boundary between the rough (trabeculated) and smooth parts of the right atrium.**

## Understanding it
- The crista terminalis is the **junction** between the two RA parts (and site of the SA node).

>> Ridge between rough and smooth RA.
opts: The ridge between the rough and smooth parts of the right atrium
The boundary of the left atrium

cards.q: What is persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC)?
cards.a:
**The left anterior cardinal vein fails to regress, leaving a left-sided SVC that usually drains into the coronary sinus.**

## Understanding it
- Failure of the **left anterior cardinal** to regress leaves a **left SVC** (often draining to the coronary sinus).

>> Left anterior cardinal persists → left SVC.
opts: A left SVC from failure of the left anterior cardinal vein to regress

cards.q: What is a coronary sinus ASD?
cards.a:
**An unroofed coronary sinus open to the left atrium, creating a shunt between the atria.**

## Understanding it
- An **unroofed coronary sinus** connects LA to RA (via the sinus) = a form of ASD.

>> Unroofed coronary sinus → atrial shunt.
opts: An unroofed coronary sinus open to the left atrium (a shunt)

cards.q: How does the left atrium get its smooth wall?
cards.a:
**By absorbing the pulmonary veins — the LA grows an outgrowth that meets and incorporates the pulmonary venous trunk.**

## Understanding it
- The LA's smooth wall comes from **absorbed pulmonary veins** (mirroring the RA absorbing the sinus horn).

>> LA smooth wall = absorbed pulmonary veins.

cards.q: How many pulmonary vein openings result, and why?
cards.a:
**Four — as the original single pulmonary trunk is absorbed, its four branches become separate openings.**

## Understanding it
- Absorbing the common pulmonary trunk to its **four branches** leaves **four openings**.

>> Four openings (from the absorbed four branches).
opts: Four — the absorbed trunk's four branches become the openings

cards.q: What is the origin of the smooth wall of each atrium?
cards.a:
**Right atrium — from the absorbed right sinus horn; left atrium — from the absorbed pulmonary veins.**

## Understanding it
- Smooth walls: **RA from the sinus horn, LA from pulmonary veins**.

>> RA smooth ← sinus horn; LA smooth ← pulmonary veins.
opts: RA smooth from the sinus horn; LA smooth from the pulmonary veins
RA from pulmonary veins; LA from sinus horn

cards.q: Where does the conduction system develop from?
cards.a:
**Specialised cells in the right atrium, close to where the sinus venosus connects.**

## Understanding it
- The conduction tissue arises in the **sinus venosus region of the RA** — which is why sinus venosus defects can cause arrhythmias.

>> RA near the sinus venosus.
opts: Specialised cells in the right atrium near the sinus venosus

cards.q: What two structures does the conduction system form and their functions?
cards.a:
**The AV node (delays the atrial signal before the ventricles) and the Purkinje fibres (rapidly conduct the impulse through the ventricles).**

## Understanding it
- AV node = **delay**; Purkinje fibres = **fast ventricular spread**.

>> AV node (delay) and Purkinje fibres (fast conduction).
opts: The AV node (delays the signal) and Purkinje fibres (fast ventricular conduction)

cards.q: What is partial versus total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage?
cards.a:
**Partial (PAPVD) — some pulmonary veins drain to the wrong place (RA/SVC/IVC); total (TAPVD) — ALL pulmonary veins drain to the systemic venous side, so no oxygenated blood reaches the LA directly.**

## Understanding it
- Partial = **some** veins misconnect; total = **all** do (a cyanotic emergency).

>> Partial = some veins wrong; total = all veins wrong.
opts: Partial = some veins misconnect; total = all veins misconnect

cards.q: Why is total APVD a surgical emergency?
cards.a:
**Because oxygenated blood never reaches the left side of the heart directly — the baby depends on a shunt (e.g. ASD) to survive.**

## Understanding it
- In TAPVD, **no pulmonary venous return reaches the LA**; survival needs an atrial shunt → urgent surgery.

>> No oxygenated blood reaches the LA → emergency.
opts: It has no effect on oxygenation
Oxygenated blood never reaches the left heart directly
It causes only a mild murmur

cards.q: Why can sinus venosus defects cause arrhythmias?
cards.a:
**Because the conduction system develops from the sinus venosus region, so defects there disturb the SA node/conduction tissue.**

## Understanding it
- The conduction tissue shares the **sinus venosus origin**, so defects there provoke arrhythmias.

>> Conduction tissue arises there → defects cause arrhythmias.
opts: They have no link to rhythm
The conduction system arises from the sinus venosus region

cards.q: How does ventricular septation differ from atrial septation in direction?
cards.a:
**In the atria the wall grows downward from the roof; in the ventricles the muscular septum grows upward from the apex/floor.**

## Understanding it
- Atrial septum grows **down from the roof**; ventricular septum grows **up from the floor**.

>> Atria: top-down; ventricles: bottom-up.
opts: Ventricular grows down; atrial grows up
Atrial septum grows down from the roof; ventricular septum grows up from the floor

cards.q: From how many components is the ventricular septum assembled, and name them.
cards.a:
**Four: the inlet, the outlet, the trabecular/muscular part, and the membranous part.**

## Understanding it
- Four contributions (**inlet, outlet, muscular, membranous**) — the multiple joints explain why VSD is common.

>> Inlet, outlet, muscular, membranous.
opts: Inlet, outlet, trabecular/muscular, and membranous parts

cards.q: Why is VSD the most common congenital heart defect?
cards.a:
**Because the ventricular septum is assembled from four separate components, giving many junctions where fusion can fail.**

## Understanding it
- **Four components = many potential failure points** → VSD is the commonest CHD.

>> Multi-component assembly → many failure points → common VSD.
opts: The septum never forms at all
It is caused by a single gene
It is assembled from four components with many fusion points

cards.q: Describe the membranous septum and its clinical importance.
cards.a:
**It is the last part to close and the smallest — a tiny fibrous patch just below the aortic valve; most VSDs are perimembranous (occur here).**

## Understanding it
- The **membranous** part closes **last** and is the **commonest VSD site** (perimembranous).

>> Membranous = last to close; commonest VSD site.
opts: First to close; VSDs never occur here
Last to close, smallest; the commonest VSD site (perimembranous)

cards.q: What is the cono-truncal region made of?
cards.a:
**Two stacked segments: the bulbus cordis (conus, lower) and the truncus arteriosus (upper).**

## Understanding it
- Cono-truncal = **conus (bulbus cordis) + truncus arteriosus** — the outflow that must be divided.

>> Bulbus cordis (conus) + truncus arteriosus.
opts: The bulbus cordis (conus) and the truncus arteriosus

cards.q: What must the cono-truncal region be divided into?
cards.a:
**The aorta (for the left ventricle) and the pulmonary trunk (for the right ventricle).**

## Understanding it
- The single outflow must split into **aorta (LV) and pulmonary trunk (RV)**.

>> Into the aorta (LV) and pulmonary trunk (RV).
opts: The aorta (LV) and the pulmonary trunk (RV)

cards.q: Why does the cono-truncal septum grow in a spiral?
cards.a:
**Because in the adult heart the pulmonary trunk spirals around the aorta; the spiral septum reproduces this crossing relationship.**

## Understanding it
- A **spiral** septum creates the normal **crossing** of the great arteries.

>> Spiral septum → the great arteries cross correctly.
opts: The great arteries normally spiral/cross, so the septum spirals
To keep them straight and parallel

cards.q: What defect results from straight (non-spiral) cono-truncal division?
cards.a:
**Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) — aorta off the RV and pulmonary trunk off the LV.**

## Understanding it
- A **straight (non-spiral)** septum → **TGA** (great arteries connected to the wrong ventricles).

>> Straight division → TGA.

cards.q: What is the role of neural crest cells in cono-truncal septation?
cards.a:
**They migrate into the region, populate the aorticopulmonary ridges, and drive the septation of the outflow tract.**

## Understanding it
- Neural crest cells **build the aorticopulmonary septum** that divides the outflow.

>> Neural crest populates the aorticopulmonary ridges (septation).
opts: They populate the aorticopulmonary ridges and drive outflow septation

cards.q: What defects result from failed neural crest cell migration in the outflow tract?
cards.a:
**Truncus arteriosus and Tetralogy of Fallot.**

## Understanding it
- Failed neural crest migration → **truncus arteriosus and TOF** (and other cono-truncal defects).

>> Failed neural crest → truncus arteriosus and TOF.
opts: Truncus arteriosus and Tetralogy of Fallot

cards.q: Why are outlet VSDs often associated with cono-truncal anomalies?
cards.a:
**Because the cono-truncal septum also grows down to close the outlet part of the ventricular septum, so its failure causes both.**

## Understanding it
- The **same septum** closes the outlet VSD and divides the outflow → failure links them.

>> The cono-truncal septum also closes the outlet VSD.
opts: The cono-truncal septum also closes the outlet ventricular septum
The atrial septum closes the outlet

cards.q: Give the mechanism of Truncus arteriosus.
cards.a:
**Complete failure of aorticopulmonary ridge fusion — a single common arterial trunk overrides both ventricles.**

## Understanding it
- No septation of the outflow → **one common trunk** (truncus arteriosus).

>> Failed aorticopulmonary fusion → one common trunk.
opts: Failed aorticopulmonary ridge fusion — a single common trunk

cards.q: Give the mechanism of Tetralogy of Fallot.
cards.a:
**Unequal division of the conus — the pulmonary side gets too little, causing pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD and RVH.**

## Understanding it
- **Unequal (anterior) conal division** narrows the pulmonary outflow → the four features of TOF.

>> Unequal conal division → pulmonary stenosis + TOF features.
opts: Unequal conal division (small pulmonary side) → the four TOF features

cards.q: Give the mechanism of Double Outlet RV.
cards.a:
**Abnormal wedging plus failure of neural crest cell migration — both great arteries arise over the RV.**

## Understanding it
- DORV = **failed wedging + neural crest failure**, so both great vessels sit over the RV.

>> Abnormal wedging + neural crest failure → DORV.
opts: Abnormal wedging plus neural crest migration failure

cards.q: From what do the great vessels develop?
cards.a:
**Six paired arterial (aortic) arches that form sequentially around the pharynx.**

## Understanding it
- The great vessels derive from the **six pairs of aortic arches** (most regress).

>> Six paired aortic arches.
opts: Six paired aortic (arterial) arches around the pharynx

cards.q: What is the general fate of the aortic arches?
cards.a:
**Most regress (like scaffolding removed after use), keeping only the parts needed for the adult great vessels.**

## Understanding it
- Only a **few** arches persist; the rest **regress**.

>> Most regress; a few persist as great vessels.
opts: Most regress; only selected parts persist as great vessels

cards.q: What does the 3rd aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**The common carotid artery, the external carotid, and the proximal internal carotid artery.**

## Understanding it
- 3rd arch → **carotid system**.

>> 3rd arch → carotids.

cards.q: What does the left 4th aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**Part of the arch of the aorta.**

## Understanding it
- The **left 4th** arch → the **aortic arch** (why the arch is left-sided).

>> Left 4th → aortic arch.
opts: Part of the arch of the aorta

cards.q: What does the right 4th aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**The most proximal segment of the right subclavian artery.**

## Understanding it
- The **right 4th** arch → **proximal right subclavian artery**.

>> Right 4th → proximal right subclavian.

cards.q: Why is the aortic arch left-sided in normal adults?
cards.a:
**Because only the left 4th arch persists to form it (the right 4th becomes the subclavian).**

## Understanding it
- The **left 4th arch persists** → left-sided aortic arch.

>> Only the left 4th arch persists.
opts: Only the left 4th arch persists to form it

cards.q: What does the 5th aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**Nothing — it regresses completely (or never fully forms).**

## Understanding it
- The **5th arch** leaves **no adult derivative**.

>> 5th arch → nothing.

cards.q: What does the left 6th aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**The proximal left pulmonary artery and, distally, the ductus arteriosus.**

## Understanding it
- **Left 6th** arch → **left pulmonary artery + ductus arteriosus**.

>> Left 6th → left PA + ductus arteriosus.
opts: The proximal left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus

cards.q: What does the right 6th aortic arch become?
cards.a:
**The proximal segment of the right pulmonary artery only (the distal part regresses).**

## Understanding it
- **Right 6th** arch → **proximal right pulmonary artery** (no ductus on the right).

>> Right 6th → proximal right PA only.
opts: The proximal right pulmonary artery only

cards.q: What is the ductus arteriosus and its fate?
cards.a:
**The fetal shunt connecting the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta; it closes after birth to become the ligamentum arteriosum.**

## Understanding it
- The ductus shunts blood **past the lungs** in the fetus, then closes → **ligamentum arteriosum**.

>> Fetal pulmonary→aortic shunt; becomes ligamentum arteriosum.
opts: A liver bypass; becomes ligamentum venosum
An atrial shunt; becomes the fossa ovalis
A fetal pulmonary-trunk-to-aorta shunt; becomes the ligamentum arteriosum

cards.q: What is patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)?
cards.a:
**Failure of the ductus arteriosus (6th arch) to close after birth — one of the commonest CHDs, especially in preterm infants.**

## Understanding it
- PDA = the **ductus stays open** after birth (continuous murmur; common in preterms).

>> PDA = ductus fails to close after birth.
opts: Failure of the foramen ovale to close
Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth

cards.q: What causes a right-sided aortic arch?
cards.a:
**The right 4th arch persists instead of the left.**

## Understanding it
- If the **right 4th arch persists** (and the left regresses), the arch is **right-sided**.

>> Right 4th arch persists → right-sided arch.
opts: The right 4th arch persists instead of the left

cards.q: What is an aberrant right subclavian artery, and what symptom can it cause?
cards.a:
**A 4th arch / right dorsal aorta abnormality where the right subclavian crosses behind the oesophagus, which can cause difficulty swallowing (dysphagia lusoria).**

## Understanding it
- An **aberrant right subclavian** passes behind the oesophagus → **dysphagia lusoria**.

>> Aberrant right subclavian behind oesophagus → dysphagia.
opts: A pulmonary artery defect causing cyanosis
A right subclavian crossing behind the oesophagus → dysphagia
An atrial defect causing a murmur
A left-sided aortic arch, causing no symptoms

cards.q: What is an interrupted aortic arch?
cards.a:
**A 4th arch defect producing a gap (discontinuity) in the aortic arch.**

## Understanding it
- Interrupted aortic arch = a **break** in the arch (a duct-dependent lesion).

>> A gap/discontinuity in the aortic arch.
opts: A gap (discontinuity) in the aortic arch

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of dextrocardia?
cards.a:
**The heart tube loops to the left instead of the right (abnormal looping).**

## Understanding it
- Dextrocardia = **left-ward (reversed) looping** of the heart tube.

>> Left-ward (abnormal) looping → dextrocardia.
opts: Left-ward (abnormal) looping of the heart tube

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of ASD?
cards.a:
**Failure of atrial septation.**

## Understanding it
- ASD = a **failure of the atrial septum** to form/close properly.

>> ASD = failed atrial septation.

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of VSD?
cards.a:
**Failure of ventricular septation.**

## Understanding it
- VSD = a **failure of the ventricular septum** components to fuse.

>> VSD = failed ventricular septation.

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of transposition of the great arteries?
cards.a:
**Non-spiral (straight) division of the bulbus cordis — the conal septum grows straight instead of spiralling.**

## Understanding it
- TGA = **straight (non-spiral)** cono-truncal division → great arteries on the wrong ventricles.

>> TGA = straight (non-spiral) outflow division.
opts: Straight (non-spiral) division of the bulbus cordis/outflow

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of hypoplastic left heart syndrome?
cards.a:
**Failure of migration of the neural crest cells (affecting left-heart/outflow development).**

## Understanding it
- Per this lecture, HLHS is attributed to **failed neural crest migration**.

>> HLHS = failed neural crest migration.
opts: Failure of neural crest cell migration

cards.q: What is the embryological cause of double inlet LV?
cards.a:
**Abnormal wedging and failure of neural crest cell migration.**

## Understanding it
- DILV arises from **abnormal wedging + neural crest failure** (both AV valves into the LV).

>> DILV = abnormal wedging + neural crest failure.
opts: Abnormal wedging and failure of neural crest migration

cards.q: OSPE — On a diagram of the primitive heart tube, name the regions from the venous to the arterial end.
cards.a:
**Sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle, bulbus cordis, truncus arteriosus.**

## Understanding it
- Venous→arterial order: **sinus venosus → atrium → ventricle → bulbus cordis → truncus arteriosus**.

>> Sinus venosus → atrium → ventricle → bulbus → truncus.
opts: Truncus, bulbus, ventricle, atrium, sinus venosus (reversed)
Sinus venosus, primitive atrium, primitive ventricle, bulbus cordis, truncus arteriosus
Atrium, ventricle, aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC

cards.q: OSPE — A diagram shows two atrial septa with an offset gap acting as a flap valve. Name the septa and the gap.
cards.a:
**Septum primum (the thin flap) and septum secundum (the thick muscular wall); the offset gap is the foramen ovale.**

## Understanding it
- Thin flap (septum primum) + thick wall (septum secundum), gap = **foramen ovale** (a flap valve).

>> Septum primum (flap) + septum secundum (wall); foramen ovale.
opts: Septum primum (flap) and septum secundum (wall); the foramen ovale
The crista terminalis; the fossa ovalis
The endocardial cushions; the foramen primum

cards.q: OSPE — Identify the arch derivatives numbered 3, 4 and 6.
cards.a:
**3rd = carotid system; 4th = aortic arch (left) / right subclavian (right); 6th = pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus (left).**

## Understanding it
- Remember: **3 = carotids, 4 = aortic arch/subclavian, 6 = pulmonary arteries + ductus**.

>> 3 carotids; 4 aortic arch/subclavian; 6 pulmonary/ductus.
opts: 3 = carotids; 4 = aortic arch/right subclavian; 6 = pulmonary arteries/ductus

cards.q: CLINICAL — A newborn with Down syndrome has a murmur and a single AV valve on echo. What is the defect and its embryological cause?
cards.a:
**Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) — from failure of endocardial cushion development.**

## Understanding it
- Down syndrome + single AV valve = **AVSD (endocardial cushion defect)**.

>> AVSD from endocardial cushion failure.
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot — unequal conal division
AVSD — failure of endocardial cushion development

cards.q: CLINICAL — A cyanotic newborn has the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left. What is the diagnosis and cause?
cards.a:
**Transposition of the great arteries — from straight (non-spiral) division of the outflow tract.**

## Understanding it
- Great arteries on the wrong ventricles = **TGA (straight cono-truncal division)**.

>> TGA from non-spiral outflow division.
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot — unequal conal division
Transposition of the great arteries — straight outflow division

cards.q: CLINICAL — A cyanotic child has pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD and RVH. What is the diagnosis and embryological cause?
cards.a:
**Tetralogy of Fallot — from unequal conal division / failure of neural crest cell migration.**

## Understanding it
- The four features = **TOF** (unequal conal division).

>> TOF from unequal conal division.
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot — unequal conal division / neural crest failure

cards.q: CLINICAL — A term newborn is deeply cyanosed and no oxygenated blood reaches the left atrium. What is the likely diagnosis?
cards.a:
**Total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (TAPVD) — a surgical emergency.**

## Understanding it
- Deeply cyanosed newborn with **no pulmonary venous return to the LA** = **TAPVD**.

>> TAPVD (surgical emergency).

cards.q: CLINICAL — A preterm infant has a continuous murmur and a shunt between the pulmonary trunk and aorta. What is the defect and its arch origin?
cards.a:
**Patent ductus arteriosus — failure of the 6th-arch ductus arteriosus to close.**

## Understanding it
- Preterm + continuous murmur + pulmonary-trunk-to-aorta shunt = **PDA (6th arch)**.

>> PDA from failed ductus (6th arch) closure.
opts: Patent ductus arteriosus — failed 6th-arch ductus closure

cards.q: CLINICAL — Which single cell type, when it fails to migrate, explains TGA, TOF and Truncus arteriosus?
cards.a:
**Neural crest cells.**

## Understanding it
- The unifying cause of the cono-truncal defects (TGA, TOF, truncus) is **failed neural crest migration**.

>> Neural crest cells.
